speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take over from the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I congratulate him on his excellent address and for exposing our fraudulent government's utter audacity to come forward requesting more borrowing authority to support its blank cheque style of government which we have witnessed since 1969.
I should like to point out how it all started under the Liberals in 1969. The erosion of parliamentary control over government spending has its genesis in certain parliamentary rule changes instituted by the Liberal government in 1969. In the summer of that year the government invoked closure, that is the termination of debate, to ram through Rule 75c which permits a minister to close debate where there is not agreement between all parties. That is the rule under which they did it. This rule has effectively prevented Parliament from properly scrutinizing government expenditures. Departmental estimates are shuttled off to the already overworked committees and are then reported back to the House. Thus debate on them is limited and seldom meaningful.
As well the number of votes on estimates has been reduced. This further restricts parliamentary debate on government spending. If one examines the estimates, one will see various estimates going through with "$1" marked beside them. That is how it all started. That is why we are faced with a bill to borrow $14 billion; that is why we are the largest borrowers of money in the world; that is why there is uncontrolled spending. The report of the Auditor General makes excellent reading for everyone, and certainly the report of the Lambert commission exposed the way the government has been operating since 1969. It was actually started in 1963, but it was accelerated with the rule changes in 1969.
The government will not only wallop it to us with tremendous borrowing; it will hit us with increases in the unemployment insurance premiums paid by employees and employers. They will rise by an incredible 3316 per cent. I understand some of the premiums might be increasing as much as 46 per cent to bail out the Liberal government. It will give the government an additional $1.1 billion per year of taxpayers' money.
I should also like to point out that spending will be $6.2 billion higher under the Liberals by 1983-84 than it would have been under the Progressive Conservative government and its responsible finance minister, the hon. member for St. John's

February 10, 1981
Borrowing Authority
West. The government will spend a total of $16.8 billion more between 1980-81 and 1983-84 than had been planned by the Crosbie budget. That is $1,900 per taxpayer per year.
The Liberals promised a progressive reduction in the size of the deficit, another lie. The deficit in 1983-84 will be $500 million larger than the deficit of last year and $2.7 billion larger than the projected deficit for 1983-84 in the Crosbie budget. Over the next four years, the total cash requirements of the government will be $12.7 billion higher than what was projected in the Crosbie budget. To meet these requirements the government will have to either borrow more money, thus driving up interest rates, or print more money, thus driving up inflation.
I should like to discuss the government's purchase or takeover of Petrofina. I received a copy of a letter today which was addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). It was from one of my constituents, a gentleman with 25 years of experience in the oil industry. I should like to point out what he said in his letter about this ridiculous takeover. He said:
1 was under the impression that the Canadian government wanted an involvement in the oil industry to assist private enterprise in the development of resources with the long-range objective being to make Canada self-sufficient.
Many of the objectives outlined were attainable within the present framework of government offices and regulations without becoming actually involved in the industry. As a person who has been involved in the oil industry for over 25 years, you leave me with a large question mark as to why the Government of Canada has to be involved in the service station business. Other than possibly to continue to retain the support of the NDP.
The acquisition of Petrofina does not give Canadians anygreater involvement in the research and exploration for oil. You have acquired approximately 1,200 service station outlets of which many cannot be economically operated. They are two and three bay outlets, mainly two bays, are poorly located and to obtain operators who can pay their overhead costs and make a profit, will be in many cases impossible.
You have purchased a refinery that is by oil industry standards obsolete and inefficient in design and in need of considerable maintenance and upgrading.
I hope the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will check out these points to find out just what he bought. It sounds as if he bought a pig in a poke. The letter continues:
The other so-called assets that you purchased with our money have a very debatable asset value, certainly nowhere near the price you have paid for this takeover.
I will go into that in more detail in a minute. The former owners of Petrofina are still laughing. They cannot understand how on earth the government would pay that amount of money. It continues:
It is very sad to see politicians such as yourself develop a twisted image of a good industry and become involved in the actual operation. Already we see signs of considerable overspending by Petro-Canada in the operation of the Pacific 66 Service Stations and other facilities taken over in western Canada.
I understand that one of the reasons for the involvement in the marketing of petroleum products is to have a window to look into the oil industry to determine how we make a profit.
You did not have to spend billions of dollars to do this, many of us could have explained it all to you. It is known as hard work, dedication and the freedom to express good constructive thinking processes. These are characteristics that one seldom finds in government-operated business endeavours.
That is the opinion of an expert on this purchase. Other people have done some homework and have conducted studies
into this purchase or takeover. I should like to refer to the article entitled: "Canadians will foot bill" which appeared in today's edition of the Ottawa Citizen by Dian Cohen. In part it reads as follows:
PetroCan offered $1.4 billion for Petrofina. That amounts to $120 a share, so far above the market price and even the asset value of the company that its president, Alfredo Campo, was ecstatic in his disbelief: "It's so far beyond what any company would pay for it, or what the market was indicating, that I wonder how it makes sense," said Campo.
If that is the case, why on earth did the Liberal government pay more than the market price for it? It simply does not make any sense. The article continues:
An objective economic analysis of this deal must conclude that there is nothing economic in it. Petrofina was selling for under $70 six months ago. It rose to just under $90 as the government played footsie.
Petrofina has for months been encouraging its employees to buy shares in the company.
During question period today the Minister of Energy was asked if there were any leaks. He said we should go to the Securities Commission if we have any evidence of leaks. It will be very interesting for the minister to find out why Petrofina was advising its employees to buy shares over the last number of months. There is no question that the government has leaked some information to some people. Dian Cohen goes on to indicate:
Petrofina knew it had a sucker.
Yes, Petrofina certainly had a sucker in the Liberal government, but unfortunately it is not the Liberal party's money that is paying for this lemon. It is the Canadian people who have been suckered again by another Liberal government. The article continues:
I wonder who else took advantage of the situation?
The crucial energy problem in Canada is getting the stuff out of the ground. That will not happen until the federal government realizes that the world price is much closer to the economic value of oil than its contrived price.
Surely there was a better way to spend $ 1.46 billion.
I think a better way to spend this money would be on building a natural gas pipeline to the maritimes. That would have made more sense than buying a bunch of gas stations. I would like to point out that 85 per cent of the oil which is needed in the maritimes must be imported. I will go into the cost of the importation of oil in just a minute.
Today there was mention made in question period about statements made by Mr. Hopper, the head of Petro-Canada, who wants the taxpayers to buy Petrofina. He points out in a recent newspaper article:
I would like 100 per cent of it to be paid out of that tax, in other words. I would like 100 per cent equity because we are pretty well strapped with debt.
So, Petro-Canada is pretty well strapped with debt. It has no funds with which to purchase Petrofina so the Canadian people must pay for it at the pumps. Figures bandied about have indicated that it will cost up to 3 cents a litre more for gasoline, which amounts to 13 cents a gallon. If that is the case then this year Canadians will be paying something in the range of a 50-cent a gallon increase. Mr. Hopper went on to say:
February 10, 1981

I am not looking at anyone right now. I do not know anyone who is even remotely interested in selling at fair and reasonable prices... It would not surprise me if we did not do another acquisition for two or three years.
I hope they will not "do another acquisition" again after the way this one was handled. It sounds like Mr. Hopper is very nervous. I do not think he was very much involved in this arrangement, it was more typical of the political manipulation by the Liberal government.
It was pointed out in the House yesterday by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) how much it will cost us for cheap gas and cheap energy. The hon. member said this:
The fact that the Liberal National Energy Program is counterproductive to Canada reaching energy self-sufficiency by 1990, and given the fact that under this program Canada will require 500,000 barrels of oil imports a day by 1990, at a cost of $43 billion annually to Canadian taxpayers-
That is what it will cost for cheap gas annually-$23 billion. Who does the government think it is kidding?
It is not very often one finds too many in the Liberal party with a conscience, but on occasion a couple of them crop up. Recently two members spoke out against the energy policy. They came up with some pretty good points. This subject matter was covered in a local news article, which reads:
Doubts about the federal government's National Energy Program are beginning to surface in the Liberal caucus itself.
At least two Liberal M.Ps say it's time for Ottawa and Alberta to resolve their bitter struggle over energy pricing and revenue sharing.
If domestic energy prices have to move substantially closer to world levels to get a pricing deal, Keith Penner and Dennis Dawson said in recent interviews, then so be it.
In this same article Mr. Dawson, who is the hon. member for Louis-Hebert and Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, said:
-the gap between Canadian and world oil prices "has to diminish.''
That is a very honest and straightforward statement. It is time the Liberal party stopped kidding the Canadian people that it will give them cheap gas and energy. There is no such thing in this world today. The article goes on to quote the hon. member as saying:
"There is a question of how long we can keep prices down.
Basically, 1 think that we made a commitment to keep prices below the Tory level for one year."
That actually did not happen, Mr. Speaker. The article continues:
Finance Minister Allan MacEachen, however, has said energy prices will be lower than what the Tories proposed throughout the government's term.
He is also a little off base with that remark.
The aerospace industry is another area in which the government is spending money. I support this expenditure. Unfortunately, the large amounts of money being spent in the aerospace industry are all being spent in Ontario and Quebec. With regard to the new fighter aircraft contract, the Liberals have announced that 48 per cent of the work will be done in Quebec, 39 per cent in Ontario, which leaves 12 per cent for the rest of Canada. I am very concerned about the five aerospace firms we have in Manitoba. These firms will not get in on any of the contract work, since the government keeps
Borrowing Authority
pouring the money into the east. There was an announcement some ten days ago that de Havilland will be receiving some loan guarantees. A report in The Globe and Mail in this respect had this to say:
The federal government also announced it will support the Crown-owned company with a $450 million loan guarantee that will also cover the $275 million design and development costs through the 1981-1985 period. Initial design and development costs will be $170 million .. . Financing will be done through bank loans and other lending instruments.
This is a subject which I must continue to raise, Mr. Speaker, until we receive some firm commitment with respect to some work for the five aerospace Firms in Manitoba. The east has certainly received more than its fair share.
I would also like to point out some of the excellent work The Globe and Mail has done with respect to the government's energy package. The reports are well researched and certainly point out the weaknesses in the National Energy Program. In an editorial dated February 9, 1981, The Globe and Mail had this to say:
When your heating bills rise, and your gasoline bills rise, chances are the provinces and the oil companies have nothing to do with it: you are helping to improve the federal government's cash flow and enable Petro-Canada to fly its colours from gasoline stations from coast to coast. We appear on the brink of a new definition of self-sufficiency: the government helps itself, and its take is never sufficient.
That last remark certainly seems to be the motto of the Liberal party: consumers and taxpayers in Canada must continue to pay and pay.
There are also some encouraging articles being published. A recent statement by the B.C. minister of energy, Mr. McClelland, pointed out that after a three-day fact-finding tour through Ontario, the minister:
-has come to the conclusion that Ottawa eventually will abandon its controversial energy policies and work with the provinces to achieve energy self-sufficiency.
I hope Mr. McClelland knows what he is talking about. That is something which all of us can go home tonight and pray for, that this ridiculous energy program will be withdrawn. Experts and authorities from across the country have pointed out that this program is counterproductive to Canada becoming energy self-sufficient.
It is not just Alberta which has been hit. There are oil companies and plants in Saskatchewan which have also suffered. The latest energy package has priced Lloydminster crude out of U.S. markets. This is a type of heavy oil which we do not have much use for in Canada. With the latest taxes imposed on this heavy oil plant in Lloydminster the product is just not saleable to the United States. A recent article in the Alberta Report of January 23, 1981, pointed out:
Heavy oil producers in Saskatchewan, already reeling under the load of provincial royalties and the new federal taxes imposed in the October budget, were hit with another blow this month. The National Energy Board, in its monthly price-setting ritual, determined that heavy oil exports were "deeply undervalued" and advised energy minister Marc Lalonde that a hefty 30 per cent increase in the federal export charge was warranted. U.S. consumers, however, found the board's so-called "just and reasonable export price" anything but. They promptly cancelled orders from their Canadian producers, who were left scrambling to find either new buyers or storage for their oil. Producers are appealing to the NEB to reconsider its opinion.

February 10, 1981
Borrowing Authority
The government has not left anybody out and it is hitting from all angles. Just to wrap it up, I would like to quote a gentleman who has helped expose the irresponsible mismanagement of financial matters by Liberal governments, Mr. Don McGillivray of Southam News, who wrote in one of his articles:
Here's the record: 1970 was the last year when the federal budget was in the black with a surplus of $500 million resulting from $14.1 billion in revenue and $13.6 billion in spending.
The budget deficit was $400 million in the fiscal year ending in 1971, $700 million in 1972 and nearly $1 billion in 1973. It reached $1.4 billion in 1974 and $1.6 billion in 1975.
At that point it was still manageable, but in the past five years revenue growth has stalled while spending has surged ahead:
In fiscal year 1976, the gap between the two was $5.3 billion; in 1977, $6.1 billion-
And on it goes. Mr McGillivray went on to say:
The upward march of the deficit faltered in the 1979-80 fiscal year when the federal government was $11.5 billion in the red but resumed in the present fiscal year. MacEachen forecast a deficit of $14.2 billion last April, the net result of $45.6 billion in revenue and $59.8 billion in spending.
In layman's terms, the Liberals are spending well over $1 billion per month more than what is taken in in revenue. It is a ridiculous and irresponsible position for this country, but there seems to be no end. We keep hearing the ridiculous statements which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first made in 1968 when he said that we would have endless inflation if we do not control spending. But his word means absolutely nothing. On the campaign trail, the Liberals said that they would control spending, but they have absolutely no intention of doing any such thing and the figures will bear me out. I have here an article which I took from the Citizen. Although it is about the Prime Minister, I believe it applies to all Liberals who, while on the campaign trail, like to give out the odd true statement:
Pierre Trudeau scraped the bottom of his barrel when he told a Brandon audience: "Whenever I see bankers, oil company presidents and newspaper giants argue we are doing something wrong, then I think we must be doing something right."
What fatuous nonsense. If the best the Prime Minister can do to try to sway audiences is to use simplistic rhetoric the like of which hasn't been heard since the Winnipeg strike, then he should keep his mouth shut.
At the time bankers were expounding the need for a proper cash flow for small Canadian oil firms. Their comments had nothing to do with multinationals or oil barons, but small oil producing firms which were suffering a reduced cash flow and as a result were leaving for the United States. For example, recently at Coutts, Alberta, there was a mile-long lineup of oil industry trucks waiting to cross into the United States. It has a new energy policy which makes it worth while for these firms to drill marginal wells and go into the tough areas, unlike the National Energy Program.
There is no way Canada will achieve energy self-sufficiency under this program. The Financial Post of recent date carried an article entitled "Don't Hinder Mining's Growth". I hope the government will not introduce the same program in mining as it has in oil. I also hope the minister of energy for British Columbia knows what he is talking about when he says that
the Liberals will have a second look at their National Energy Program, because it is having devastating effects on this country. I hope the government will search its conscience and withdraw this ridiculous program as soon as possible.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-59, which enacts the Borrowing Authority Act for 1981-82, allows the government to obtain an additional $14 billion in loans to finance public works and for general purposes. While the statutory provision is short and simple, the effect of the action authorized is extensive and complex in both human and economic terms. There is no magic involved in borrowing. Everyone knows that whatever is borrowed must be returned.
In the case of Bill C-59, what the government proposes is to borrow money-vast sums of money. There will be a clear requirement that those vast sums of money must be repaid in the times specified and, more importantly, that interest will be paid during the term of the loan. Those Canadian home owners who face renegotiation of their mortgages in 1981 and those Canadians who must replace their automobiles or acquire furniture or equipment know all about paying high interest rates. They know the devastating effect of increased monthly payments on the family budget.
Do hon. members know what will happen to a family with a home mortgage which expires this month? Let us suppose that the mortgage was granted in 1976 when interest rates were relatively low and that the interim payments have reduced the principal amount owed to $40,000. If the interest rate was 9 per cent, the monthly payment required to pay off the loan in 25 years would be $331. But with an interest rate of 15.5 per cent, the monthly payment would be $513, a difference of $182. By current standards, an interest rate of 15.5 per cent for a residential mortgage is considered good. A Canadian home owner might well be faced with a 16.5 per cent rate which, on a $40,000 mortgage, would add $27 to the monthly payment. It would bring the increase to over $200 per month.
Let us consider the increase in home mortgage costs at this level in the context of general inflation. Canada has experienced an inflation rate and a consumer price index increase in the 10 per cent range over the past years. If this 10 per cent inflation rate were applied to a $331 mortgage payment for five years, the resulting increase would approximate the same amount. That is, a $331 mortgage payment with a 10 per cent yearly increase over five years would rise to $530 so the total increase is approximately $200.
The point is that what Canadians are experiencing in a variety of ways, including mortgage rates, is the effects of inflation. For most people, the real question is whether their incomes have kept pace with galloping inflation. Keeping pace will allow them to maintain but not improve their standard of living.
Applying the same 10 per cent rate, a wage earner receiving $15,000 in annual income in 1976 should be earning approximately $24,200 annually today, otherwise he or she is falling
February 10, 1981

behind the annual inflation rate. While I have applied a 10 per cent inflation rate to mortgage payments, I can assure Canadians that it can be applied with similar effect to most consumer goods and services.
There are, of course, exceptions, some of which are notable. The electronics industry, for instance, has kept price increases in line and the price of some primary food items has not increased with the inflation rate. By and large, Mr. Speaker, consumers are paying for inflation in the cost of the goods and services required for basic needs.
When a family's income falls below expenditures it has two choices: it can reduce spending by cutting back on the goods and services purchased or it can borrow to meet the deficit of expenditures over revenue. I can understand the reluctance of Canadian families to cut expenditures on goods and services as in most cases it means reduction in the standard of living and in such essentials as food, clothing, home shelter and transportation.
We know that borrowing money in order to meet a deficit will result in more problems. Many Canadian families whose incomes have not kept pace with inflation, face a difficult decision. Those faced with a budget deficit can make a choice whether to cut back on expenditures or to borrow. The Canadian government has made the choice for the national family and that choice is to borrow the funds needed to pay the difference between national revenues and national expenditures.
How times have changed. I remember in the early fifties reading an editorial reprinted from the New York Times that compared the state of the United States economy to that of Canada. At that time the United States was resorting to deficit financing but the Canadian government was budgeting for a respectable surplus. The editorial suggested the United States government should follow Canada's example and reduce expenditures to equal revenues. Now the situation seems to be reversed and the President of the United States has faced the American people with the hard economic facts. Government spending has eroded their economic strength and President Reagan has issued a challenge both to government officials and the people to face the problems and solve them. The president has placed reliance on the private sector and plans to reduce taxation, in the belief that the taxpayers will generate economic activity. At the same time, he plans to cut back on government services and promote the kind of self-reliance that made the United States a strong nation. Like the rest of us President Reagan realizes that some people need assistance and I am sure he will continue with that kind of essential service to those who cannot provide for themselves.
In Canada, things are different. Instead of positive action our government has set up a constitutional smokescreen and has introduced a bill in Parliament to authorize the borrowing of $14 billion. It has taken no steps to reduce the drain on the national economy. The money is being spent to provide services the citizens of Canada do not want.
Let me review the historical facts that brought about this problem in the national economy and which brought us to the
Borrowing Authority
current position of requiring borrowing authority in the range of $14 billion. We must bear in mind that this is in addition to a borrowing authority passed in July, 1980, in this House by which the government was authorized to borrow $12 billion for that fiscal year.
There is now an accumulated budget deficit of $69 billion. I do not need to tell anyone what a drain on the national economy a deficit of that magnitude is. What has gone wrong, Mr. Speaker? I think the problem goes back to 1970 when Canada had a buoyant economy and government revenues and expenditures were in line and within reasonable limits. Reacting to that economic situation, the government began looking for ways of spending the public funds being accumulated. It sought to establish programs that had appeal for some segments of the population and which resulted in vast and extensive payments. Under the existing law the provincial governments, and not the federal government, were required to meet those payments. In those days of wine and roses, the late sixties and early seventies, the federal government began to involve itself in areas that were primarily of provincial concern. There is the established programs fund through which the federal government provides funds for what are essentially provincial services. It is now seeking to reduce the amount provided to the provinces.
Just recently the community services program has been cancelled. The federal government became involved in that area in the 1970s when revenues were high and funds easily available. Now it seeks to absolve itself of responsibility for community service and it has cancelled that program.
That is not all the government has done. It is now changing agreements that have been in force and in place for many years. I have particular reference here to the agreement respecting the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Many years ago, when some of the provinces did not have a provincial police force, the federal government offered the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Because it was in the interests of the federal government at the time, those services were highly subsidized by the federal authority. With the pinch of inflation, with eroding revenues in comparison with expenditures, the federal government now seeks to withdraw that service and it seeks to fine the provinces with all the cost of the service although it is claimed that the formula now being considered contains a substantial amount of federal subsidy. The cost to the provinces of providing the service the Royal Canadian Mounted Police used to provide for them will be a further financial drain.
The change in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police agreement, the cancellation of the community services program and the changes in the established programs fund are all an indication that the federal government is facing the result of its actions over the past ten years. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I might proceed without further interruption on this most serious matter which exists in our society-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE ORDERS
speechtext: Do you want five minutes?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE ORDERS
speechtext:
I will accept the offer. I will accept any time that can be given. In the negotiations preceding private members' hour I pleaded with the government to allow the subject to go to a committee, but that has been denied me. I have been told that the government, once again, will talk out this important issue. Therefore, the bill will die. Nothing will ever come of it from this government. The government has had opportunities ever since 1972 to address this important matter, this important cancer which is destroying the dignity, freedom and potential life for children being reared in separated and divorced families.
That is the issue with which we are dealing today, and the warning of Solzhenitsyn is in play right here in this House at this hour. So how is it possible for a member to address something constructively on an issue as important as this, Mr. Speaker?
Bill C-250 deals with a problem which has been around for a long time. It affects children being reared by single parents who are experiencing continuous stress in their daily lives and
7092

February 10, 1981
Alimony and Maintenance
who are struggling because the maintenance orders of family courts are not being enforced. I have personal experience of working wives who, bringing up three children, are almost breaking down trying to maintain some kind of standard of living, some kind of style and self-respect in putting their children through the educational process in this country. I am sure every person in this House knows of cases of such breakdowns and knows of the breakdown in the process of carrying out the maintenance orders from the courts of this land.
What this bill is trying to address is a system whereby the courts will enforce the orders. What we are trying to put in place is legislation which would remove the haven for people who have been given court orders to assist in the maintenance of their children in the case of a family breakdown. What is involved here is the peace of mind and mental health of mothers. Most of the people in these cases are women who are trying to raise their children without support when the court orders are not enforced. The problem is the complete, utter, shameful and disastrous degree of apathy on the part of the staff who back up the family courts because federalism in this Parliament has not worked in co-ordinating the split jurisdiction in the matter of family law. We have even heard the subject of reform of the family law brought up in the constitutional debate. We have seen the draft legislation of the provinces dealing extensively with this issue. We have seen the Law Reform Commission come down with reports in 1975 and 1977, and we have seen other working papers on this issue. We have the Canadian Bar Association's resolution number eight which was published in September of 1980 on this very issue of the garnishee powers of the court and the enforcement of court orders for the support and maintenance of children.
I should like to refer to the study paper of the Law Reform Commission of Canada entitled, "Family Law, Enforcement of Maintenance Orders". I should like to read its conclusion into the record. It reads:
Something is profoundly wrong with a body of law and practice that fails to attain its objects more often than it succeeds. Failure is the universal characteristic of the traditional system for enforcing maintenance orders in Canada. With a few notable exceptions in recent years, apathy has been the companion of failure.
I just spoke of the apathy which exists in the rooms behind the courts and of the failure of our society to enforce the support orders, the result of which is the destruction of dignity and the removal of equal opportunities for children reared in such circumstances. The Law Reform Commission of Canada continues its conclusion as follows:
The burden of this social evil is and has always been carried by women, most of whom are found in the least economically influential strata in Canada. It would be consciously avoiding identification of one of the main reasons for the present shameful situation (and we use the word "shameful" advisedly) if it was not mentioned that the voice of women has historically been virtually absent from the councils of those who designated, shaped and administered the present system.
Reform involves two courses of action. First, there must be an effort by governments in Canada to improve individual laws and practices which deal directly with maintenance enforcement. Second, the whole body of marriage breakdown law must be thoroughly reshaped.
I am not just speaking idly here. This bill has a very long history in the House. May I remind hon. members that it was a member on their side, Mr. Barney Danson who, before he became a minister of the Crown, placed this bill on the Order Paper in the Twenty-ninth Parliament. When he became a member of the government and a Privy Councillor, I went over to him and asked him whether he would mind if I, as an opposition member, picked up his initiative because of the personal experience I have had in this regard. He welcomed my suggestion, and in the first and second sessions of the Thirtieth Parliament, first readings were given and second reading debate took place on Bill C-203. A very interesting and active debate ensued, as reported in Hansard of Friday, November 26, 1976, during which it was pointed out that perhaps the bill was not in order as a private member's bill. Hon. members on the government side spoke very constructively in the debate, with the exception of one hon. member, and the matter received a very good airing.
I went back to that debate and, after studying it, I sent the record out to lawyers in the community who are concerned about the swinging-door syndrome which exists in the family courts. Mr. Donald Moir, a family lawyer in Vancouver, has volunteered hours and hours of his time, as have other lawyers, in the drafting of a bill which would address this very serious swinging-door syndrome and this disgraceful and shameful situation we have allowed to exist in our society. The draft came to me and I had to put it into a form in which it could be presented as a private member's bill in the House. I believe the parliamentary legal counsel worked on it for a period of about three weeks to put the thrust of that draft bill into a form which could be presented to the House. My hope today was that the initiative, which has now been before the House since 1972-this is the second time it has had second reading debate, and the bill has had an immense amount of background study-will be accepted by the government. My hope is that the government will see fit to have the bill withdrawn and send its subject matter to committee where we can bring in the experts of the land and where we could probably start debate on an amendment to Section 15 of the Divorce Act, as is outlined in the bill. This bill is the best effort of the concerned people who have assisted a private member in this initiative.
When the bill was before the Thirty-first Parliament, it remained in the draw because the government was going to take action on it. We all know what happened. Things have changed and the Liberal government is now back in power.
The whole matter of family law is so serious and is such a national disgrace that all of the provincial governments have prepared papers on it. The Law Reform Commission of Canada has prepared its sequence of papers, the Senate has prepared reports on it, but the House continues to frustrate the initiatives of private members and to prevent the movement of this subject matter to a committee where the government itself could pick up the initiative and do something about this shameful and disgraceful situation.
February 10, 1981

1 have personally seen women, trying to raise three children on their own, breaking down and experiencing serious health problems because of the failure of their husbands to maintain payments under a court order. I have seen them going back to the family courts to obtain an order which would provide maintenance. These orders would last only two months, following which there was no more money.
Surely to goodness in this age at this hour in this House when we talk about International Women's Year, we should address one of the most serious problems they have. I can give statistics with respect to the number of women at or below the poverty level who are in the disgraceful and shameful circumstance of not receiving support, and the courts fail to enforce support orders. I can give the House chapter and verse on three different experiences I have had in which there have been serious problems. I have seen companies-those evil businessmen we hear so much about-take on the responsibility of supporting, rearing and educating children in such circumstances.
The Law Reform Commission released a working paper on divorce in 1975. It released a working paper on the family court. In 1977 it released a paper on eligibility to attachment. I have already reminded the House of resolution No. 8 of the Canadian Bar Association. If ever there was an example of federalism not addressing the problems of a country like Canada, I think this is classic, for all the federal government has to do is take an initiative very similar to the one in this private member's bill before us. All it has to do is take such a simple initiative to overcome one of the major failures of our legalistic society. Nothing I have observed causes more loss of dignity and more intolerance for law and order than the disgraceful poverty conditions children of broken homes are reared in as a result of our inability to correct this shameful situation.
I remind hon. members that on October 16, 1979, the hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) moved a motion under Standing Order 43 on this same issue. I know hon. members opposite, including the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Irwin), know of this. I know all lawyers in this House who are skilled and versed in the nature of law and in the problems of law are aware of this problem, but where is the initiative and the will to correct this disgusting apathy we and civil servants behind the law courts and the enforcement of these orders have?
This package I have in my hand is the package of papers I have received from lawyers out in the field on this issue. This second package is the package of papers I have received from parliamentary counsel on this issue. I have the best efforts draft of the provinces, and I have papers from each of the provinces on the family issue. Most of this problem could be resolved if we in this House accepted the challenge this bill offers us, and if we moved the subject matter of this bill into a committee and took the initiative on Section 15 this bill offers, which is not an idle wish or statement. It is a considered,
Alimony and Maintenance
studied application with respect to the problem within the limits our process here allows a private member. If we could take this initiative and this subject matter and bring in the experts of the land, we could address this and give some hope and some chance to the children and the progeny of broken homes and broken marriages, a very high percentage of whom are being raised at or below the poverty level.
Quite frankly, I am surprised that the government has decided not to allow the subject matter of this bill to go to committee and that hon. members opposite will talk the bill out.
This matter has been around since April of 1974 in its various phases. It was here on February 14, 1975. It was here on November 26, 1976, when it had second reading debate and was talked out. That debate was studied. There were adjustments, and the outcome of that debate is in the bill before us today. Here again, this is not good enough. Once again the bill will be talked out, I am told. The issue will remain static and this shameful, disgusting, disgraceful condition of lack of uniformity of enforcement of separation orders will continue to exist. Back in 1976 the government said it would bring down a bill that would address this situation. The Thirty-First Parliament said it would address this situation. We are now into the Thirty-second Parliament, and we are still not going to seize on this opportunity to move this subject matter into committee so that we can get this nasty, disgusting, and disgraceful situation within our society fixed.
And we wonder why federation is not working. We wonder why there are critics of this place. This is a prime example of why the Parliament of Canada is not working. We do not accept social challenge. We do not address the needs that are out there and to which we have all been exposed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) for bringing these points to the attention of the House, as he has done so forcefully now and in the past.
I think perhaps his denunciation is too broad. We are as concerned as he is about the welfare of spouses who have to take care of their children, and about the lack of enforcement. In many cases there is no collection because there are no funds. I believe one of the seven major causes of family breakdown is lack of Finances. In many cases-although the figures are high-orders have not been enforced simply because there are no assets. A good friend who was a family court judge once said to me that it is like putting one blanket over two beds. That is the problem in collecting these finances.
However, we in this Parliament are concerned, as are a number of jurisdictions across Canada. Provincial jurisdictions are trying to come up with new and better methods of enforcing these monetary obligations. After all, if we do not collect from delinquent spouses, it is only the taxpayer who has to pay.

February 10, 1981
Alimony and Maintenance
The money is taken not only from provincial coffers but also from federal coffers because we contribute substantially to provincial payments.
The current process is found in Sections 14 and 15 of the Divorce Act, and I will read them both. Section 14 says, and I quote:
Effect of decree or order. A decree of divorce granted under this act or an order made under Section 10 or 11 has legal effect throughout Canada.
Section 15 states, and I quote:
Registration and enforcement of orders. An order made under Section 10 or II by any court may be registered in any other superior court in Canada and may be enforced in like manner as an order of that superior court or in such other manner as is provided for by any rules of court or regulations made under Section 19.
What is the effect of Sections 10 and 11 of the Divorce Act? By virtue of these sections each maintenance creditor, in whichever province of Canada he or she may be, of a Section
10	maintenance order, which is an interim order, or a Section
11	maintenance order, which is a final order under the Divorce Act, wherever made in Canada automatically has available all superior court remedies of every province for enforcement.
A point can be made that the court itself should enforce the order, police the order, hire accountants, hire collection agencies or hire any number of people within the court system to go out and collect. This suggests that the bureaucracy is better at doing a specific job than the private sector. I respectfully suggest, by itself that is not always the case, as evidenced by many of the things bureaucracies have tried to do.
What is the situation today? How can these orders be enforced? They can be enforced by at least six or seven methods which 1 can suggest: garnishment proceedings, equitable receivership, examination of judgment debtors, attachment of debt or bank accounts, seizure of personal property, execution against land and proceedings for committal. I suggest that in 50 per cent of the cases there is nothing at the end of those processes because there was nothing there at the beginning.
When the delinquent spouse decides to separate, most of the major assets are split at that time and the minor assets, which are usually few and far between, must be seized. In addition, in most of the provinces, provincial enactments permit the filing of superior court maintenance orders in provincial family courts and make these courts available to spouses. This is exactly what the hon. member is suggesting. In some cases this is a good method. In many cases there is a great deal of dissatisfaction with bureaucratic collection of funds for spouses.
Over and above this we have the traditional show cause hearings whereby the defaulting debtor is forced to come to small claims courts and explain why he has not paid or face imprisonment on summary conviction and continuing attachment of his wages. This way, indirectly, maintenance orders made pursuant to the Divorce Act in the superior court of one province may be enforced by the family court of either the
same province or any other province. Family court procedure could be made more productive by innovations, and there have been innovations. In some family courts there are automatic systems of enforcement under which the enforcement is done by the specific court on an automatic basis.
In certain provinces they have even gone further and have computerized the process. The point is, Mr. Speaker, no matter how good the process is, we still must go to the basic needs of the family. It is not the case when two millionaires divorce or split. It is at the lesser level where there is a lack of money that we have the problem. Many times the spouses are brought into small claims courts. Again, if there is nothing there, how can you collect?
What we are talking about today is basically machinery. We are all interested in better machinery. Suggestions have been made by the hon. member for Capilano. He did not, all by himself, discover the process. I assure him that many members on this side of the House have been discussing the same thing for many years. I believe the next speaker tried on at least three occasions with private members' bills to do the same thing. It is not something he discovered or solely cares about. There have been suggestions that the new Federal Court rules could be amended to provide for garnishment orders, which is a good idea. In that way you can go ex parte to the Federal Court and seek your remedy.
There have been suggestions that the Divorce Act be changed to provide for garnishment orders. This is very close to what the hon. member is suggesting. He is also suggesting the federal civil service, including senators, Members of Parliament and so on, should be exempt from any protection because they are now under the royal prerogative. I agree with him and I think the government agrees with him. The government has and is tabling effective legislation. Once it is passed, it will bring into this House exactly what the hon. member has suggested.
One attempt in May, 1978, was Bill C-49. Legislation was introduced but it died on the Order Paper. It was based on the Law Reform Commission recommendation and on the report on attachment of remuneration payable by the Crown in right of Canada.
In March, 1979, during the fourth session of Parliament, Bill C-52 was given first reading. It also failed. In June, 1980, the federal government introduced Bill C-38, the garnishment, attachment and pension diversion act, which is now being considered. The proposed legislation would, subject to certain conditions set out in the legislation, permit provincial law on garnishment or attachment to apply to moneys paid by the Crown in right of Canada for salaries, fees, honoraria and like payments in respect of their performance of services for the Crown. As I indicated, once this becomes law, federal employees, Members of Parliament, senators, judges and others could be garnisheed for maintenance and support debts as well, like any other citizen, as they should have been long ago. In addition, superannuation moneys due to retired public servants would be subject to diversion for satisfying mainte-
February 10, 1981

nance orders, which are matrimonial orders, and not ordinary debts.
In conclusion, the substance of what the hon. member opposite said is endorsed and is concurred with in the spirit but not the exactitude of what he is suggesting in this proposed legislation. We all want the best for estranged spouses. It is a matter of what mechanism we will use, the best mechanism, to reach that desired goal.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate to the House that the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) has not raised just one problem but in fact two or three. I recall having discussions before the dissolution of the Trudeau government in 1978, when this was one of the last items going down to the wire before the House was dissolved, on the question of the garnisheeing of wages of Crown employees. It is unfortunate we still have this anomaly in the books. If Canadians were aware of this anomaly they would be somewhat surprised, if not outraged, that the average citizen working in the private sector is liable for garnishee orders and that federal civil servants, Members of Parliament and senators are still immune from application of the garnishee order which is enforceable on anyone else. It is clearly an absurd situation. It is so clearly absurd that I am surprised the government has not made an effort to bring in that kind of measure at any time. It seems to be the sort of thing which, in this day and age, would be very quickly passed by the House. ! am surprised this government and the previous government did not choose to introduce that particular measure and have it voted on rather than some of the other measures which they decided to have us vote on.
They obviously chose the wrong ones. There is no reason for crying over spilt milk. We have to deal with the measure before us. 1 hope very much the government will not talk this bill out because it does deserve study. What has obviously happened-and I think the hon. member for Capilano has expressed it very well-is that family law reform has become a subject of constitutional contention. This has taken the question of the Divorce Act away. Some of the limitations in the Divorce Act and the problems in the Divorce Act have been taken away from the floor of the House of Commons and the attention of the government. Clearly, if it is the government's view-and it has been expressed by the government-that family law should be a question of provincial jurisdiction, and I can see very strong arguments in support of that proposition, then clearly the whole motive and impetus for this kind of amendment to the Divorce Act will not receive very much attention from the government. On reflection, the government should recognize there is nothing stopping it from introducing an amendment to the Divorce Act which would facilitate maintenance and alimony payments subsequent to a divorce order. I do not see why we should have to wait for the process of constitutional reform in order to get that amendment. The hon. member for Capilano expressed his frustrations. Let me assure him that I have mine and that we all have frustrations with respect to this problem. I do not see why we should wait for the ultimate resolution to the question of family law
Alimony and Maintenance
jurisdiction. In my view a fundamental principle has been expressed in the piece of legislation put forward by the hon. member for Capilano. The principle is that it should be possible, without the continual necessity of returning to court time and time again, to get an order upon every default which can be immediately enforced and will provide for maintenance and alimony payments to the dependent spouse.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Irwin) made an important point, that there is an assumption behind the whole area of alimony and support payments and their relationship to welfare, and the real problems of dependants which are created by family break-ups. I am sure all of us as members of Parliament are acquainted with these problems. There is an assumption that the so-called supporting spouse actually has something and that it is simply a question of finding a speedy way to get the courts to act, apparently that will produce the solution. I can think of the problems I have dealt with firsthand in my constituency. In many, many cases the real problem is much more profound-"there ain't nothin' there". One can enforce all the orders one wants on the departed spouse, but if the departed spouse cannot be found, if he has managed to tie up his affairs in such a way that there is no way of getting at them or, if one sees that there is really nothing there, then clearly the human problems described so eloquently by the hon. member, which all of us recognize as being very real, will still be there. Perhaps this is where the philosophies of the hon. member for Capilano and myself about dealing with this problem differ; perhaps that is where we part company.
Having said that and having indicated our support, it seems to me there are two solutions to the problems. One solution might be called the best solution, that is, that we make fundamental decisions on the questions of where family law should be and who should be responsible for it. We should attempt to unify the world of divorce, separation orders, court orders, maintenance orders and property orders as best we can. The questions on whether one goes to the supreme court in one's jurisdiction for a divorce, whether one goes to the family court for a separation arrangement or whether the enforcement of separation orders is different than the enforcement of alimony and maintenance payments under divorce judgments must be changed.
Although I understand many groups are unhappy about the idea of any federal jurisdiction over the area of family law being taken away, on the basis of the evidence we have heard, it is perhaps one of the first areas which most Canadians could agree should be handled in a unified manner at the provincial level. I should like to borrow the words of a political philosopher: In many cases the best solution may be the enemy of what is clearly good in the bill before us.
It could be five or ten years before we reach constitutional agreement on what should be done about family law. Until we reach that solution, we must do everything we can to facilitate

February 10, 1981
Alimony and Maintenance
the enforcement of maintenance and alimony payments subsequent to divorce orders. That is the reason I hope the government will not decide to talk out this bill, but will refer it to committee where it can be studied. 1 think we will Find a fair amount of agreement in committee among all members of the House; we want to reduce the technical objections a spouse can mount for his failure to make alimony and maintenance payments. We want to make it as easy as possible for dependent spouses to have orders enforced. Also, we want to make it possible for dependent spouses to have their orders enforced by way of garnishee orders on all Canadian citizens, whether or not they are employees of the Crown.
In summary, the problem stems from the fact that in a sense we are in the middle of a constitutional question. We should not allow the constitutional question to ignore the very real human problems which exist and have been shown to exist by everyone who has studied or looked at this problem. The proposals of the hon. member for Capilano go some way toward finding a partial solution to the problem. We should consider adopting this partial solution until such time as a final resolution is found for the question of where family law decisions should be made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to speak on the bill in the name of the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) which deals with continuing garnishees for alimony payments in divorce actions. Unfortunately, it is necessary to debate this subject, but I compliment the hon. member for Capilano for not only introducing the bill, as he has done in other years, but for his persistence in pursuing the matter. Over the years he has not let the matter drop and has made certain that our attention was refocused on this very important subject.
Briefly I should like to refer to one of the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission. As indicated in the explanatory notes in the bill, the commission recommended:
The rights of family dependants should no longer be ignored merely on the basis of legal anachronisms-
On the basis of legal anachronisms, we cannot allow the hurt and pain in our society to continue because of our inability to deal legislatively with those problems. This is not a matter of politics. There should be no politics in these subjects which are of immediate human dimensions. I have experienced the reward of seeing the subject matter of a private member's bill go to committee. I applauded then and 1 do so today when the government looks past the politics of a matter and moves to the heart of it, which involves the people in question, allowing subject matters such as this to be taken to committee, whether it be justice and legal affairs or health and welfare, as it was in the case of my presentation. In the committee these human problems can be dealt with by people who deal with them daily. It is a place where legal testimony can be given.
In Canada something in the order of one out of every three marriages ends in divorce. I understand that in the United States the figures for marriages ending in divorce are approaching one out of two. Behind those statistics, Mr. Speaker, lie the untold thousands of cases of anguish, of people who are left on tenterhooks because they cannot reach the kind of settlement which is their due.
I know of one case, and I am sure the hon. member for Capilano is also aware of it, which involves a marriage break-up. In this case the husband left, moved to another province and then returned. He was well-to-do and had plenty of resources.
He was called upon by the court to pay alimony and child support. He would refuse to pay this money until the former spouse went before the court to collect it. Then, on the last day, he would make that payment to the court. He would wait long enough before paying the money to force her to pay out most of it in legal fees. The next month he would do the same thing. In euphemistic language, this is called a "legal anachronism". It is a polite way of dealing with this matter on the floor of the House of Commons. It is legal jargon, but in the lives of people who are affected by this legal anachronism it is far from adequate.
When we view the statistics with respect to marriage breakdown in our society today, we must admit that our structure is breaking down. As someone said to me some time ago, it is far too easy to get married. He said it ought to be more difficult to get married and easier to obtain a divorce. To obtain a driver's licence we must first have had some driver training. The potential driver must demonstrate his ability to drive. In order to get married all you have to do is go to the court house, get a licence, show that you are of age and physically healthy. There is no preparation for the development of interpersonal relationships, how to handle family finances, how to build organic family units or how to handle stress in a family. We really do not prepare people the way we ought to.
We must admit that in our society we have not taught people to accept accountability for their decisions. Instead, we are teaching people to cop out from the responsibility and the decisions in their lives. Because people have been able to do
February 10, 1981

this for a long time, they feel that after they have been married, then divorced, they can then cop out. Somewhere along the line we must assume responsibility for those who refuse to be accountable and make them learn the lesson of accountability.
We have terms like "no fault insurance". Maybe there is a place for that kind of insurance, but I wonder about the name "no fault insurance". We have been teaching people that no one is at fault. We now have terms like "creative divorce". How can you have creative divorce when at least two people will be hurt? How can that be creative?
This bill puts the emphasis where it ought to be, on the person who has been directed by court order to pay child support or alimony and who is now trying to walk away from that responsibility. The hon. member for Capilano is doing us a service by bringing this matter to the attention of the country. I trust the government will see that this is not a political issue, but a very human one. I hope the government will allow the subject matter of this bill to be brought to the committee, whether it is justice and legal affairs or health and welfare. At this point that is not material. What is material is that we have an opportunity to study in depth the matter the member for Capilano has brought before us. This would allow the government to obtain the kind of evidence which is needed and later on a bill could be presented to the House, based on further evidence which could be built upon the work that the hon. member has already done.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank my colleagues for giving me this opportunity to speak on a topic which is dear to me. I must say how very happy I am to see that my Progressive Conservative colleagues are also concerned about social issues. They even want more bureaucrats to solve a problem. To my mind, they will certainly not settle it through a measure under which women will continue to be the victims of a system forcing them to appeal to the courts and behave like beggars asking for handouts to which they are fully entitled to begin with.
Mr. Speaker, Quebec's Bill 183, an act to promote the payment of support, with which 1 am more familiar, received royal assent on June 18, 1980, and is being enforced by a network of administrative offices throughout the province. I also know that Ontario has set up a similar organization and that the provinces are about to enter this field, since they recognize that the problem relates to social affairs and primarily falls under provincial jurisdiction.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that my colleague is interested in the lot of divorced women and children generally. However, the bill ignores separated women and their children, as well as common-law wives and their children. That is why 1 suggest that this bill is woefully inadequate and does not meet the current needs of Canadian women. Without insisting on the jurisdictional aspect of the problem, just the same 1 should
Alimony and Maintenance
like to point out to my colleague that negotiations have been under way since 1979 to reach agreement with a view to transferring to the provinces legislative powers over divorce, and that question was also on the agenda during the intensive negotiations held last summer. The transfer of social affairs or family law to the provinces is still on the agenda.
Therefore, on the eve of an agreement with the provinces, 1 suggest it would be altogether premature to adopt a measure which in fact would do precious little other than create one more administrative organization at a time when two provinces whose residents constitute over half the people of Canada already have a system to ensure the payment of support.
I can inform the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) that this system already exists in Quebec, where it is working very well. Many people are satisfied with the new legislation which has been introduced, which is more relevant to the civil code than to the jurisdiction of the federal government. I do not wish to protect women's rights through a new administrative mechanism, but I would like them to have the opportunity to collect money which in most cases is for their children and to be ensured they will receive that money regularly.
In fact, Germany has a minimum amount which is actually paid by the state. The spouse is required to pay the state the difference between the state minimum standard and the actual alimony or maintenance order payments. Denmark has a similar system. A minimum amount is paid for each child and that amount is ensured. Women do not have to beg for this money, nor is the court required to intervene. This system is working very well.
What we are dealing with is the very narrow scope of divorce. I hope the hon. member will take another route, perhaps through legislation that deals more with income security which has the effect of protecting all persons, and will take the advice of his colleague from British Columbia who says that we should not try to attain perfection. I am not trying to attain perfection, but I would like to see decent legislation which deals with the problem with which many women have been living for years.
I believe we are very close to solving this problem by having the provinces deal with the matter. Of course, the federal government can help by establishing the system in other provinces. 1 do not believe the Department of Justice will withdraw its support, but I presume that most of the provinces can as easily establish the same system which already exists in Ontario and Quebec to ensure the collection of maintenance. This would eliminate the need to establish an administrative body at the federal level, which would only have the effect of complicating the situation.
Because of the reciprocal agreement between Ontario and Quebec, women of either province may have their maintenance orders enforced if the spouse has moved from one province to

Borrowing Authority
the other. Bill C-250 is very laudable, but it limits the possibilities and may create certain problems. I do not see why the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs should continue to study the problem when it is very well known. I ask the hon. member for Capilano and the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) to think on the scale of the revenue problems which women in general face in Canada. Certainly, this very partial measure would not provide that the spouse pay money to the person and members of the family who are to receive the support.

Mr. Speaker, that is why I think that the claim of a person entitled to support more properly falls under provincial rather than federal legislation. We would only add confusion to the current situation if we were to endorse a measure that in fact would duplicate others which are about to be adopted. I simply wish that my two friends opposite would help us expedite passage of Bill C-38 on the recovery of alimony payments and all debts owed by civil servants.
